question.problem: John selected a pair of socks out of his drawer without looking in the drawer. He has $5$ pairs of black dress socks, $4$ pairs of brown dress socks, $10$ pairs of black sports socks, and $3$ pairs of white sport socks. What is the probability of selecting a pair of black socks or a pair of sports socks?
question.worked_solution:
Let us call $B$ the event "a pair of black socks has been selected," and $S$ the event "a pair of sports socks has been selected." Then the probability of selecting a pair of black socks or a pair of sports socks is $P(B\cup S),$ and we can apply the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B\cup S)=P(B)+P(S)-P(B\cap S)\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's find $P(B),$ $P(S),$ and $P(B\cap S).$

- There are $5+10=15$ pairs of black socks among the $5+4+10+3=22$ pairs of socks, so we have

$$
P(B)=\frac{15}{22}.
$$

- There are $10+3=13$ pairs of sports socks among the $22$ pairs of socks, so we have

$$
P(S)=\frac{13}{22}.
$$

- There are $10$ pairs of black sports socks. So, we have

$$
P(B\cap S)=\frac{10}{22}.
$$

Therefore, applying the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B\cup S) & =P(B)+P(S)-P(B\cap S) \\  & =\frac{15}{22}+\frac{13}{22}-\frac{10}{22} \\  & =\frac{18}{22} \\  & =\frac{9}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$
